submitLabel: Your register, the inventory, and the write-up
intro: Paste the register (eight to twelve decisions, six columns), the inventory of AI capabilities live in your stack, your predicted count scored against what you found, and the 300–400 word write-up including your position on this module's claim. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext: You are grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, People Ops & HR Technology track — for People Operations, HR Operations, HRIS and HR Systems professionals who have completed AI 101 and AI 201. Module 1 applied activity, 'The register': the artifact the whole eight-module track runs on. The learner produces (a) a register of eight to twelve recurring decisions their function actually makes, each with six columns — volume, reach (how many people one wrong instance touches), detection latency (immediately / next payroll / annual audit / compliance filing / in litigation / never), reversibility (effort and blast radius of undoing it, not whether an undo button exists), current accountability BY NAMED PERSON, and defensibility (whether that person could reconstruct the rationale); (b) an inventory of AI capabilities live in their stack right now, each with who decided, when, and on what evidence, explicitly including features that arrived switched on inside systems they already owned; and (c) a single chosen decision the remaining seven modules will run on. The module's core distinction is that a task audit lists things to automate while a decision audit lists things somebody has to defend, and its diagnostic question is 'can you name the person — not the team — who would defend this?' CRITICAL GRADING INSTRUCTION: blank and 'nobody' and 'don't know' entries are the intended finding of this exercise, not defects. A register with honest gaps must score ABOVE a register with no gaps, because a complete register is almost always a guessed one. Specifically reward the learner who resisted resolving an empty accountability cell by naming a team — the module states that a team cannot sign anything. Do not reward volume: twelve rows with real latency values beat forty with plausible ones, and a learner who submitted eight well-evidenced rows should score at the top. The module's claim, which the write-up must take a position on, is that the organization's AI adoption number is mostly a description of what vendors shipped rather than what the function chose; its real counter-argument is that this is true of all enterprise technology and has never been a problem — nobody evaluates tax-table updates or TLS versions — so the honest concern is narrower, that only capabilities which make or shape a decision about a person need a gate, and the learner must say where that line falls and who draws it. A learner who concludes 'case by case, I'll know it when I see it' has described themselves as the gate rather than building one, and the write-up should be pushed on that. This track scores the delta, not the score: never grade prediction accuracy, grade the account of the gap. Note also that for some learners 'go and check' genuinely cannot settle the opening claim — release notes may be inaccessible, or the systems estate may be owned by IT. That is a finding, not a failure: score it at full credit where the learner states specifically what they could not access, why, and what they would need in order to answer it.

opening.label: Predicted — AI capabilities live in your stack today
opening.hint: Every feature that generates text, ranks, recommends, answers, or scores. Count before you look.

calibration.label: Actual — how many you found
calibration.hint: Include the ones that arrived switched on in systems you already had.

calibration.label: Of those, how many you can name who decided
calibration.hint: A person, not a team. Zero is a common and useful answer.

dimensions.name: The rows are decisions, not tasks
dimensions.criteria: Each row must be something that was decided — an eligibility rule, a routing or approval threshold, a picklist definition, an exception path, a tolerance — rather than an activity the team performs. The test: could this row be challenged, and would defending it require a rationale rather than a procedure? Rows that are really tasks ('process new hires', 'run the merit upload') score low even when described in detail. A learner who converted an apparent task into the decision underneath it — asking what was decided in order for the task to have its current shape — should score at the top.

dimensions.name: Reach and latency are answered honestly, not optimistically
dimensions.criteria: Reach must be the population affected by a SINGLE wrong instance, not the population the decision applies to overall. Latency must name a real detection event — next payroll, the annual audit, a compliance filing, litigation, or never — rather than a vague 'quickly'. 'Never' appearing at least once is a strong signal of honesty; a register where everything is detected immediately is a register that has not been examined, and should be pushed on. Credit the learner who names what specifically would fire for each short-latency row.

dimensions.name: Accountability is by name, and blanks survived
dimensions.criteria: The graded behaviour is resisting the urge to fill the accountability column. Empty cells and 'nobody' entries are the intended output and must score ABOVE a fully populated column. A learner who wrote a team name where the honest answer is nobody has removed the finding, and should be told so directly. Also credit the defensibility column doing separate work — a named owner who cannot reconstruct the rationale is a distinct risk from no owner at all, and a register that collapses those two has lost a distinction the track uses later.

dimensions.name: The inventory found what arrived through door one
dimensions.criteria: The valuable part of the inventory is capabilities that arrived switched on inside systems the organization already owned — release-note features nobody procured. An inventory listing only deliberately purchased AI tools has found door two and missed the module's point. Credit specifically: reading release notes as evidence, naming features the learner did not know were enabled, and honest 'who decided: nobody / unknown' entries. Where the learner could not access release notes or does not administer the system, credit a specific account of that blocker over a guessed list.

dimensions.name: The chosen decision can carry seven more modules
dimensions.criteria: The selected decision must be live, observable by this learner, and one where an AI capability is already involved or imminent. A decision they cannot watch, or one owned entirely by another function, will strand them by Module 3. Credit a stated reason for the choice that references the register's own columns — 'this is the one with wide reach and no named owner' is the intended reasoning.

dimensions.name: The delta and the position
dimensions.criteria: The predicted capability count against the actual, with an account of what the gap reveals — an undercount with a specific cause (features enabled by default, a system they do not administer) is the intended finding and scores at the top; so does a defended accurate prediction from someone who genuinely tracks this. Accuracy is never graded, only the account of the gap. Plus a committed position on the module's claim that engages its real counter-argument: that consuming vendor improvements without individual evaluation is normal and correct for enterprise technology, so the defensible line is narrower — only capabilities that make or shape a decision about a person. A position that resolves this as 'case by case' should be marked down for describing the learner as the gate rather than building one.
